steps.title: Install pandas and load orders.csv
steps.instructions: In the empty workdir run `uv init .` and `uv add pandas`, download orders.csv from https://github.com/techwithtim/PanadasTutorial into it, then in main.py import pandas as pd, load df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv') and print(df). Run `uv run main.py` to see the [40 rows x 9 columns] summary.

targets.caption: Import pandas with the conventional pd alias
The printed DataFrame summary: 40 rows x 9 columns

explanations.topic: Installing pandas with pip or a uv virtual environment
Why pandas is imported as pd
DataFrame vs Series
CSV files and two-dimensional data
read_csv loads a file into a DataFrame

hints: Make sure orders.csv is in the same folder you run the command from.
Your file needs three lines: the import, a pd.read_csv call, and print(df).
Run it with `uv run main.py` so the virtual environment that has pandas is used.
Look at the last line of output: it should read something like [40 rows x 9 columns].
common_mistakes: Running `python main.py` outside the uv environment, giving ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'.
Forgetting `uv add pandas` after `uv init .`.
orders.csv saved in a different folder (or downloaded as an HTML page), causing FileNotFoundError or parse errors.
Typo like pd.readcsv or pd.read_CSV.
Naming the script pandas.py, which shadows the pandas library.
steps.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')
print(df)

steps.title: Load the CSV in a Jupyter
steps.instructions: Create notebook.ipynb next to orders.csv, and in the first cell import pandas as pd and set df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv'). Run it, then run print(df) in a second cell.

targets.caption: First cell: import pandas and load the CSV into df

explanations.topic: Why use a Jupyter notebook instead of a plain .py file for pandas
Creating a notebook via Command Palette (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P, 'New Jupyter Notebook') or a .ipynb file
Installing the VS Code Python extension to get notebook support
Notebook cells run independently; df stays loaded between cells
Running, executing above/below, deleting cells and clearing outputs

hints: Open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P / Cmd+Shift+P), choose 'Create: New Jupyter Notebook', and save it as notebook.ipynb next to orders.csv.
In the first cell write `import pandas as pd` and `df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')`, then click the run button and select a Python kernel.
Add a new cell below with `print(df)` and run only that cell. df is still in memory from the first cell.
If VS Code can't open notebooks, install the 'Python' extension from the Extensions pane. If the import fails, run `pip install pandas` in the kernel's environment.
common_mistakes: Saving the notebook somewhere other than the folder containing orders.csv, causing FileNotFoundError.
Running the print(df) cell before running the read_csv cell, giving NameError: name 'df' is not defined.
Choosing a kernel/interpreter that doesn't have pandas installed (ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas').
Not having the VS Code Python/Jupyter extension, so 'New Jupyter Notebook' doesn't appear.
Typing pd.readcsv or pd.read_CSV instead of pd.read_csv.
steps.run_command: Run cell 1 (pick a Python kernel when prompted), then run cell 2
steps.code:
# cell 1
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')

# cell 2
print(df)

steps.title: Explore the DataFrame
steps.instructions: In new cells of notebook.ipynb run df.head(), df.tail(), df.info(), df.describe(), df.columns and df.index to inspect the data.

explanations.topic: head() shows the first five rows
tail() shows the last five rows
info() gives entries, columns and dtypes
Why text columns show as object dtype
describe() generates descriptive statistics
columns lists column names
index is a range from start to stop by step

hints: Add a new cell below the one where you loaded df, and try df.head() first.
head(), tail(), info() and describe() are methods and need parentheses. columns and index are attributes and take no parentheses.
Put each command in its own cell, so the notebook shows each result.
If you get a NameError, re-run the cell that creates df with pd.read_csv first.
common_mistakes: Calling df.columns() or df.index(), which fails because they are attributes and not methods.
Writing df.info without parentheses, which only prints the bound method.
Running the cells after a kernel restart without re-running the import and read_csv cell, which gives a NameError for df.
Putting several expressions in one cell, so only the last one is displayed.
steps.run_command: Run each cell in the Jupyter notebook (Shift+Enter)
steps.code:
df.head()

df.tail()

df.info()

df.describe()

df.columns

df.index

steps.title: Select columns and rows
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb select a column with df['Country'] and several with df[['Country', 'Product']]. Select rows by position with df.iloc[0] and df.iloc[10]['Country'].

targets.caption: Selecting a single column returns a Series
A list of columns returns a DataFrame
Pick a row by position, then a value by column

explanations.topic: A single-column selection returns a pandas Series
Built-ins like len() and set() work on a Series
Selecting a list of columns returns a new DataFrame
iloc selects rows by integer position
A row can be indexed by position or by column name

hints: Run df.columns first to see the exact column names you can select.
Use one set of brackets for one column, df['Country'], and double brackets for several, df[['Country', 'Product']].
For rows, use df.iloc[n] with square brackets, not parentheses.
Chain a column name onto a row to get a single value: df.iloc[10]['Country'].
common_mistakes: Writing df['Country', 'Product'] with single brackets, which raises a KeyError. Use a list inside: df[['Country', 'Product']].
Calling iloc like a function, df.iloc(0), instead of df.iloc[0].
Misspelling or miscasing a column name (e.g. 'country'), which raises a KeyError.
Expecting df.iloc[1] to return the first row, when positions start at 0.
steps.code:
df.columns
df['Country']
len(df['Country'])
set(df['Country'])
df[['Country', 'Product']]
df.iloc[0]
df.iloc[10]
list(df.iloc[10])
df.iloc[10][0]
df.iloc[10][1]
df.iloc[10]['Country']

steps.title: Filter rows with conditions
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb filter rows with boolean masks combined by & and |, e.g. df[df['Quantity'] > 2]. Also filter with .str.startswith('A') and ~df['Country'].isin([...]).

targets.caption: String method filter on Customer Name

explanations.topic: Boolean mask: df[df['col'] == value] selects only the rows where the condition is True
Combine conditions with a single & wrapped in parentheses, not Python's 'and'
Use a single | (pipe) for 'or' conditions
Comparison operators like >, <, <= and != also work as filters
.str accessor gives string methods such as startswith and endswith
isin matches against a list of values, and ~ inverts the condition

hints: Put a condition inside df[...]: df[df['Category'] == 'Electronics'].
To combine conditions, wrap each one in parentheses and join them with & (and) or | (or).
For text columns, use .str.startswith('A') on the column. Then pass the result into df[...].
To exclude values, use df[~df['Country'].isin(['USA', 'Sweden', 'Brazil'])].
common_mistakes: Filtering the wrong column, e.g. 'Product' instead of 'Category'. You get an empty table instead of an error.
Using Python's 'and'/'or' instead of & and |. This raises 'The truth value of a Series is ambiguous'.
Leaving out the parentheses around each condition when combining with & or |. Operator precedence then causes errors.
Writing .startswith directly on the Series instead of .str.startswith.
Case mismatches: endswith('A') finds nothing because the names end in lowercase 'a'.
Misspelling column names such as 'Customer Name' (with the space), which causes a KeyError.
steps.code:
df[df['Category'] == 'Electronics']
df[(df['Category'] == 'Electronics') & (df['Country'] == 'USA')]
df[(df['Category'] == 'Electronics') | (df['Country'] == 'USA')]
df[df['Quantity'] > 20]
df[df['Quantity'] > 2]
df[df['Customer Name'].str.startswith('A')]
df[df['Customer Name'].str.endswith('a')]
df[df['Country'].isin(['USA', 'Sweden', 'Brazil'])]
df[~df['Country'].isin(['USA', 'Sweden', 'Brazil'])]

steps.title: Update values with loc
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, update rows with `df.loc[<condition>, 'Column'] = value` (e.g. replace USA with United States in Country). Then uppercase a text column with `df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper()` and print it.

targets.caption: Locate rows by a condition, then pick the column to update

explanations.topic: loc locates rows by label or condition, iloc by integer position
loc returns a DataFrame because several rows can match
df.loc[condition, column] = value updates matching rows in place
Bulk-update all rows where Country is USA
Vectorised string methods: .str.upper() on a whole column

hints: Use df.loc[condition, 'ColumnName'] = new_value. The condition picks the rows and the second item picks the column.
The condition looks like df['Country'] == 'USA'. Put it inside loc's square brackets, then add a comma before the column name.
For uppercase, assign the column back to itself: df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper().
Re-run a filter cell after each change to confirm it worked, e.g. df[df['Country'] == 'USA'] should now come back empty.
common_mistakes: Writing df.loc[...]['Product'] = 'Tim' (chained indexing). This triggers SettingWithCopyWarning and may not update df.
Misspelling the column name, e.g. 'Product Name' instead of 'Product', or the wrong case for 'Customer Name'. This adds a new column or raises KeyError.
Using iloc with a boolean condition and a column label instead of loc.
Calling df['Country'].upper() without .str, which raises AttributeError.
Running .str.upper() without assigning the result back to df['Country'], so the column is unchanged.
Filtering for 'United States' after uppercasing and getting no rows, because the values are now 'UNITED STATES'.
steps.code:
df.loc[df['Customer Name'] == 'Anna ...']
df.loc[df['Customer Name'] == 'Anna ...', 'Product'] = 'Tim'
df.loc[df['Customer Name'] == 'Anna ...']

df.loc[df['Country'] == 'USA', 'Country'] = 'United States'
df[df['Country'] == 'USA']
df[df['Country'] == 'United States']

df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper()
df['Country']

steps.title: Drop rows and clean data
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, drop a row with `df = df.drop(<index>)` and check with `df.tail()`, then reload the CSV. Try `df.dropna()`, `df.fillna(...)` and `df.rename(columns={...}, inplace=True)` using your CSV's real column names.

targets.caption: Fill missing values instead of removing

explanations.topic: drop removes a row by its index label
dropna removes rows containing null/NA values
fillna replaces missing values with a given value
inplace=True modifies the existing DataFrame instead of returning a new one
Renaming columns with rename(columns=...)

hints: drop takes an index label; assign the result back with df = df.drop(...) or nothing changes.
Use df.tail() after dropping to see the last rows and confirm the index is missing.
fillna and rename accept a dict: {'column': value} and columns={'old': 'new'}.
The key in rename must match your CSV's column name exactly; check df.columns first.
common_mistakes: Calling df.drop(39) without reassigning to df, so the row is still there.
Running the drop cell twice, which raises KeyError because index 39 no longer exists.
Using a rename key that doesn't match the actual column name, so nothing gets renamed and no error appears.
Forgetting inplace=True on fillna/rename and expecting df itself to change.
Expecting dropna() to change the row count when the data has no missing values.
steps.code:
df = df.drop(39)
df.tail()

# (reload the CSV: df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv'))

df.dropna()

df.fillna({'Order ID': 0}, inplace=True)

df.rename(columns={'OrderID': 'Order ID'}, inplace=True)
df

steps.title: Analyze, group and save data
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, run `value_counts()` on a column, `groupby(...)[...].sum()` and `sort_values(..., ascending=False)`. Save the result with `df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False)`.

targets.caption: Save the DataFrame to a new CSV

explanations.topic: value_counts counts occurrences of each value in a column
groupby works like SQL GROUP BY, then aggregate with sum
sort_values with ascending=False sorts descending
to_csv and the index parameter

hints: Each operation goes in its own cell. Start with the column you want to count, then call .value_counts() on it.
For grouping, chain the calls: df.groupby('Country') then select ['Price'] then call .sum().
Sorting uses df.sort_values('Price', ascending=False). Saving uses df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False).
If you get a KeyError, check that the column names match your CSV's headers exactly, including capitalization.
common_mistakes: Calling df.value_counts('Country') or misspelling it as value_count instead of df['Country'].value_counts().
Forgetting the parentheses on .sum() so a method object is printed instead of totals.
Typing 'Ascending=False' with a capital A, or passing ascending as a string 'False'.
Writing df.2csv or df.toCSV instead of df.to_csv.
Omitting index=False and ending up with an extra unnamed index column in new_file.csv.
Using a column name that differs from the CSV header (e.g. 'country' vs 'Country'), which raises a KeyError.
steps.run_command: Run each cell in the Jupyter notebook (Shift+Enter)
steps.code:
df['Country'].value_counts()

df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum()

df.sort_values('Price', ascending=False)

df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False)
